head:
Health · Bones and skeleton

Bone: a capital built before age 30

Nobody looks at their bones before they break. Yet a large part of what your skeleton will be at 70 is decided in the years when you jump, run and grow. This article follows a single question, from the broadest view to the most precise: does the adult skeleton really depend on what is built when young, and what remains possible later?

The problem

Osteoporosis is talked about as a grandmother's disease, one that arrives after 60. Calcium is talked about as a children's matter, with plenty of dairy products. In between, almost nobody tells a teenager or a young adult that their skeleton is being built right now, that it will not keep building indefinitely, and that what is not laid down at 20 is not easy to catch up on afterwards.

The idea is simple: bone is a living tissue, constantly being made and broken down. During growth, making wins out and bone mass increases. Then comes a high point, called peak bone mass. After that, the balance slowly shifts towards loss. If this picture is right, what you have at the peak determines the height from which you start to come down. If it is too simple, you need to know that.

This picture raises several problems. At what age is the peak, exactly? You often read “around 30”, and we wanted to check that before writing it. What raises the peak: diet, sport, genes? And if you are past the age of growth, is it over?

The question

Is your adult skeleton fixed by what you build before 25 or 30, what really builds it, and what remains possible afterwards?

We proceed in six steps, from the general to the specific: the trajectory of a skeleton over a lifetime, what builds it during growth, what late loss costs, what diet does and does not provide, what remains possible in adulthood, and then the objections. The answer comes after that.

What is at stake

What is at stake is, first of all, independence. A hip fracture at 80 is not a local event: one year later, some patients can no longer walk without help, and some die within the year (figures at step 3). It is the consequences that make bone worth an article, not density in itself.

It is also a question of numbers. In France, around 484,000 new fragility fractures were estimated for 2019, and the figure is expected to rise to 610,000 in 2034, which is 26% more. Across Europe (the 27 EU countries, plus the United Kingdom and Switzerland), there were 4.3 million fractures of this type in 2019.11 Worldwide, up to 37 million fragility fractures occur each year in people over 55, about 70 per minute, and one woman in three and one man in five over 50 will have an osteoporosis-related fracture.10

Finally, there is a question of timing that is specific to this subject. For most health factors, you can start at any age. For bone, the period when it is built fastest is short, and it comes before anyone thinks about their bones. If you are a parent, teacher or coach, you are in charge of that period. If you are 20, you are at the end of it. If you are 40, the question becomes: what can still be done? Getting it wrong in either direction costs either years of lost building or needless guilt.

Step 1 of 6 · The trajectory of a skeleton

Bone mass rises fast during growth, levels off, then slowly declines

We start with the general shape. The skeleton is not built at a constant speed. The Canadian research programme Pediatric Bone Mineral Accrual Study has followed children and adolescents since 1991: 251 children aged 8 to 15 joined the study between 1991 and 1993 and were followed for 26 years. Girls reach their maturation on average at 11.8 years, boys at 13.4 years.5 The researchers explain that the largest gains in bone mass occur over a period of up to five years around the growth spurt, and that the bone mass gained at that time is double the amount that will be lost late in adult life.4

It remains to locate the peak. The sources read do not all give the same wording. The National Osteoporosis Foundation press release accompanying its 2016 statement says that peak bone mass is typically reached “in the early twenties”.2 The International Osteoporosis Foundation compendium says “around the mid-twenties” and specifies that the peak is determined “to a large extent during the first two decades of life”.3 None of the pages read gives “30 years” as the age of the peak.

Bone mass rises until the early twenties, then gently declines

Qualitative diagram, not a data curve: only the positions of the growth spurt (11.8 and 13.5 years, Saskatchewan programme) and of the peak (early to mid-twenties, NOF and IOF) come from the sources. The actual amplitude varies by skeletal site. Sources: usask.ca, NOF 2016, IOF.2,3,4

What this means

Most of the building takes place during childhood and adolescence, with a peak speed around the growth spurt. After that, there is a margin of a few years, then the peak. This curve is not yours, it is the average shape: the peak varies by site (hip, spine, whole body), by sex and from person to person. Remember the order of magnitude: the decade that matters most for bone capital is the one from 10 to 20.

If the shape is right, the next question is what raises the peak. It is not a chance of nature: part of it depends on what you do.

Step 2 of 6 · What builds bone

During growth, what matters most is loading and impact

In 2016 the American National Osteoporosis Foundation published a position statement on the development of peak bone mass, based on a review of the literature since 2000. It concludes that lifestyle choices influence 20 to 40% of adult peak bone mass, and that the strongest evidence (grade A) concerns two factors: calcium intake and physical activity, especially in late childhood and puberty.1,2 The rest depends on other factors, including genetics: you do not choose everything.

For physical activity, let us look at one specific trial. A Swiss team randomised 28 classes of first and fifth grade (children of about 6-7 and 11-12 years): 16 classes (297 children) received daily physical education lessons including at least 10 minutes of jumping or strength exercises, and 12 classes (205 children) served as controls. Of the 380 children who had agreed to the measurements, 275 (72%) had complete data after the intervention.6

Jumping during the school day builds bone

Gain of the intervention group compared with controls, as reported in the article abstract; no absolute value in grams. All significant (p below 0.05 for content, 0.01 for density). Source: Meyer et al., Bone, 2011.6

What this means

These children did not do high-level sport: they added about ten minutes of jumping and strengthening to their day. BMC is the amount of mineral in the bone, BMD its concentration per area; both rise. The effect does not differ between girls and boys, but it is larger before puberty.6 The same finding appears in a meta-analysis of 16 school-based trials in children aged 5 to 17: exercise programmes targeted at bone improve the mineral content of the whole body and lumbar spine, but the effect at the femoral neck is not significant in this synthesis (about 1 trial in 3 was at high risk of bias).7

Jumping is not only a school matter. In 89 prepubertal children, seven months of high-intensity jumping had already produced a gain in bone mass at the hip; after seven months without it, the children in the jumping group still had 4% more mineral content at the femoral neck than the controls.9 What remains years later is the subject of the next step, after looking at what loss costs.

Step 3 of 6 · What late loss costs

The higher you start, the more margin you have: and a 10% loss matters a great deal

To understand why the peak matters, you have to look at what loss does. The International Osteoporosis Foundation gives two reference points. A 10% loss of bone mass at the hip can come with a hip fracture risk multiplied by 2.5. A 10% loss of vertebral bone mass can double the risk of vertebral fracture.10 These are associations, but they show the scale of what is at stake for a few percent.

In the other direction, the IOF compendium cites two estimates: a 10% increase in peak bone density would delay the onset of osteoporosis by 13 years, and in children, a peak that is 10% higher would reduce the risk of osteoporotic fracture in adulthood by 50%.3 These figures are cited by the IOF from other work that we did not open: they are modelling estimates, not results of a trial that followed children until the age of fracture. They indicate a direction, not a guarantee.

What a fracture costs is better documented. Hip fractures weigh the most, because they occur mainly after a fall: more than 95% of hip fractures are caused by a fall, and nearly 75% occur in women.10

One year after a hip fracture, many do not regain their independence

IOF values one year after a hip fracture. The categories overlap (they cannot be added together), and the mortality bar shows the high value of the stated range (up to 20 to 24%). Source: IOF, epidemiology of osteoporosis and fragility fractures.10

What this means

These figures describe older people, who rarely have their first fracture at 30. But they explain why the stake is not “having nice bones”: it is not becoming dependent after a fall. The bone peak is what gives you margin. That does not change the fact that a fall remains a fall: fractures also have to do with balance, muscular strength, eyesight, medication. Bone is only one part of the risk.

If capital is built with impact, it remains to see what diet adds to it. This is the question everyone asks first, and it is approached with caution.

Step 4 of 6 · Diet

Calcium and vitamin D support the building, they do not replace it

This section describes what the literature says, not what you should do: needs vary from person to person, and a health professional is the right person to discuss them with.

The National Osteoporosis Foundation statement ranks calcium intake among the two factors with grade A evidence, together with physical activity. Vitamin D has good evidence of a positive role, and dairy consumption also has good evidence. Conversely, sugary fizzy drinks have good evidence of an unfavourable effect on bone building. For many other factors, the authors say rigorous trials are lacking.1,2

The calcium intake reference values quoted in the press release are those of the American Institute of Medicine: 700 mg per day from 1 to 3 years, 1,000 mg from 4 to 8 years, 1,300 mg from 9 to 18 years, 1,000 mg from 19 to 30 years.2 These are the reference values of one country and one era, not individual medical thresholds. The press release also cites other nutrients useful to bone (fibre, potassium, magnesium, vitamin C) and food sources: dairy products, oily fish, fruit, leafy vegetables, foods fortified with calcium and vitamin D.2

What this means

Calcium is the raw material, impact is the signal that tells bone to use it. A sufficient intake does not make bone strong if mechanical stress is missing, and the reverse is also true. The data read do not allow conclusions about supplements for a given person: that question is for a health professional. No figure in this section is dosage advice.

So far, everything has been about youth. But most readers of this article are no longer children.

Step 5 of 6 · After growth

In adulthood, weight-bearing training slows loss and can add a little

Let us start with the adult before the menopause. In a 1996 Finnish trial, 98 sedentary women aged 35 to 45 were randomly assigned to a group doing progressive impact exercise three times a week for 18 months (49 women) or a control group (49). Femoral neck density, a weight-bearing site, increased by 1.6% in the trained group and by 0.6% in the controls (significant difference). At the distal radius, a bone that does not bear body weight, there was no significant difference (−1.5% versus −0.7%).12 This illustrates a principle: bone responds to stress where it is applied.

A meta-analysis of 6 trials (256 premenopausal women) concludes in the same direction: impact exercises of under 30 minutes increase the density of the femoral neck (standardised difference of 0.64) and of the trochanter (0.36), but not that of the lumbar spine (0.04, no effect).14

After the menopause, the question becomes one of loss. A meta-analysis of 75 studies, with 5,300 participants, finds significant but modest effects of exercise on bone density: a standardised difference of 0.37 at the lumbar spine, 0.33 at the femoral neck and 0.40 at the total hip. The authors stress that results vary greatly depending on the protocol, which they attribute to poorly dosed programmes.16 Another synthesis, of 25 trials of at least 24 weeks, arrives at differences of 0.29 at the femoral neck and 0.18 at the spine; from these the authors derive an estimated reduction in the relative risk of fracture over 20 years of about 11% and 10%, an estimate that is modelled and not measured.15

What this means

A standardised difference of 0.3 to 0.4 is a modest effect: exercise does not rebuild a skeleton, it limits the loss and gains a little, mainly at the hip for impact. This effect is smaller than the one seen in children, which fits with step 2: the moment when bone responds best is also the moment when it is being built.

The most precise long-term study is the German Erlangen programme (EFOPS): women in early menopause with osteopenia, followed for years. A first analysis over 12 years compared women according to how often they trained.18

Two sessions a week or more: bone density stops falling at the spine

Change in bone density (DXA) over 12 years, women in early menopause with osteopenia. Groups: 16 women at 1.5 to under 2 sessions per week, 25 women at 2 to 3.5 sessions, and controls; allocation made after the fact (retrospective analysis). Source: Kemmler and von Stengel, Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2014.18

What this means

Women who trained 1.5 to under 2 times a week were not distinguishable from women who did not train. Those who trained 2 to 3.5 times a week kept their density at the spine, and lost less at the hip. The authors conclude that a frequency of at least two sessions a week might be necessary. Important caveat: the groups were formed after the fact, on small numbers, so other differences between these women (motivation, health) are not ruled out.

The same group then followed 67 women for 16 years (39 trained, 28 controls), with an assessment every 4 years.17

The gap between trained women and controls keeps growing over 16 years

Bone density gap (DXA) between 39 trained women and 28 controls, women in early menopause with osteopenia, measurements at 4, 8, 12 and 16 years. Not both sites are significant at every time point. Source: Kemmler, Engelke and von Stengel, J Bone Miner Res, 2016.17

What this means

The benefit did not fade, which is what the authors had feared: at the spine, the gap goes from 2.4 to 4.5 points, at the femoral neck from 0.9 to 3.0. This is not a gain compared with baseline (the controls lose): it is a gap in loss. And it comes from a single supervised programme, with women followed closely, which is not your everyday life.17 Earlier in the same programme, over 26 months, the lumbar spine on DXA had changed by +0.7% in the trained women and by −2.3% in the controls.19

All this looks like a conclusion. It is not one yet: we need to look for what contradicts it.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What holds up when you try to demolish the result, and what remains uncertain

Objection 1: children's gains do not last

This is the most serious objection. In the follow-up study of the hip in children who had jumped for seven months, the researchers followed 57 of them for almost 8 years (33 “jumpers” and 24 controls, i.e. 47% of the starting group).8

The gain from jumping shrinks over the years, without disappearing

Difference in hip bone mineral content (BMC) between children in the jumping group and controls. At 8 years, the difference is adjusted for age, height, weight and physical activity. Source: Gunter et al., J Bone Miner Res, 2007 (abstract).8

What this means

A gain of 1.4% that persists after eight years is small and fragile: a little over a third of the initial gain, in under half of the starting children. It does not say that childhood impact is useless (the children kept growing and moving, and the gap remains significant), but it rules out writing that a few months of jumping “secure” the adult skeleton. The initial gain erodes, and the activity that follows matters. None of the trials read follows children until the age when fractures occur.

Objection 2: adult gains fade too

In the women aged 35 to 45 in the Finnish programme, a 3.5-year follow-up after training stopped shows that the structural advantages at the femoral neck (cross-sectional area, section modulus) were no longer significant. However, leg power (+5.1%) and estimated VO2max (+4.6%) remained higher than in the controls.13 The skeleton adjusts to the current load: what you stop stressing is lost.

Objection 3: is every type of exercise equivalent?

No, and the syntheses do not agree. A network meta-analysis of 49 trials (3,360 postmenopausal women) ranks combined endurance and strength training first for the lumbar spine and femoral neck, but finds no significant effect of impact exercise alone at the femoral neck, which contrasts with the 1996 trial (although that one involved non-menopausal women).22 The possible reasons (populations, protocols, age) are not settled in the abstracts read. One cautious rule can be drawn: combining loading and impact seems safer than betting on a single type.

Objection 4: density is not fracture

Almost all the studies in this article measure bone density, not fractures. Density is a useful indicator, but it does not tell the whole story: bone quality, muscular strength and falls also matter. In the ACTLIFE trial on 54 women in early menopause, thirteen months of intense high-velocity training improved lumbar spine density (significant difference from controls) but not hip density, and another report from the same trial at 28 weeks found no significant effect on the spine (standardised difference of 0.26).20 Finally, a meta-analysis of 1,248 postmenopausal women concludes that antiresorptive drugs add to the effect of exercise: exercise and treatment are not substitutes.21 Treatment is a matter for the doctor.

Objection 5: what about the “peak at 30”?

We looked for it. The NOF statement and the IOF compendium speak of the early to mid-twenties, and the PBMAS programme followed children aged 8 to 15 for 26 years.2,3,5 We could not open the 2011 article by Baxter-Jones (“Bone mineral accrual from 8 to 30 years of age”): it is blocked from reading. The peak varies by skeletal site, and the time when it occurs is not a precise date for each person. “Before 30” is therefore a cautious upper bound, not a proven peak age: the title states it as an order of magnitude.

The answer to the problem

The question had three parts. Here are the answers, with their degree of certainty.

Is the adult skeleton fixed by what is built before 25 or 30? Largely, yes, but not entirely. This is the best-established part: the greatest share of bone mass is acquired during childhood and adolescence, with a peak in the early or mid-twenties according to the sources read, and a lifestyle that explains 20 to 40% of the peak (NOF). What is more fragile: the exact figure for the peak, which varies by site, and the estimates that a peak 10% higher would delay osteoporosis by 13 years, which come from models.

What builds it? Solid: impact physical activity and calcium intake, at the time of growth. A randomised school trial (275 children analysed) shows mineral content gains of 4.7 to 5.5% depending on the site, and a meta-analysis of school trials points the same way. Less solid: how long these gains last, which decreases over time (3.6% at 7 months, 1.4% nearly 8 years later), and the share of each of the other factors.

What remains possible later? A lot less than as a child, but not nothing. Probable: weight-bearing and impact training slows loss or adds a little, mainly at the hip, provided it is regular (two sessions a week or more in the Erlangen study) and continued. Uncertain: the effect on fractures themselves, which no trial read measures, and the best type of exercise, on which the syntheses diverge.

The most honest summary: bone is built young, with impact, and then maintained by continuing to stress it. No age is too late to limit loss, no age is too early to lay down the capital.

What to put in place

The following actions are ordered. The retest frequency is an editorial choice, not study data. The test on this page measures a physical capacity, not your bone density: it does not replace a medical examination.

  1. If you are a parent, teacher or coach: put impact into children's week.Jumping, running, ball games, strengthening: the Swiss trial added at least 10 minutes of jumping or strength work to a school day.6 The NOF press release cites, for building the peak, reference values of at least 3.5 times body weight at impact, 100 impacts per session, 3 days a week, for at least 7 months. The authors also acknowledge that the ideal dosage is not well established: treat these figures as orders of magnitude.2,1
  2. If you are between 15 and 30: keep loading.The peak is in the early or mid-twenties. Impact sports (running, jumping, team sports) and strength work with weights fit the logic of what the studies show. No study read gives a precise programme for this age: training should stay regular rather than exceptional.
  3. After 30: keep two sessions a week or more.In the Erlangen study, the threshold that stands out is two weekly sessions or more, in postmenopausal women.18 Combining loading and impact seems safer than a single type of exercise (objection 3). If you have known osteoporosis, pain or a fracture risk, get medical advice first.
  4. Do not forget diet.Calcium and vitamin D support the building but do not replace mechanical stress. Dosage and supplements are a question for a health professional.2
  5. Redo the test on the page every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.It does not measure bone, but it tells you whether your ability to jump, run or lift is improving, and therefore whether the load you impose on yourself is real. It is the thread linking this page to the article.

Unusual bone pain, a fracture without significant impact or a family history of osteoporosis justify medical advice before changing your programme.

What these figures do not say
  • The trials measure bone density or mineral content, not fractures. Most involve women (menopausal or not) or children of both sexes; adult men are poorly represented in the sources read.
  • The gains observed in children decrease over the years; no trial read follows children until the age of fractures.
  • Several figures cited by the IOF (a peak 10% higher) come from models. They indicate a direction, not a measured result.
  • This article does not replace medical advice, particularly on dietary supplements and on treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Is my skeleton “finished” at 30?

No. The peak of bone mass is in the early or mid-twenties according to the sources read, but bone renews itself throughout life, and weight-bearing activity remains associated with less loss after the menopause.3,16

Are dairy products enough?

They are among the factors for which the NOF notes good evidence, along with calcium and vitamin D, but impact physical activity is the other factor with grade A evidence. One does not replace the other.2

Do you have to jump your whole life?

The data read show that gains erode when you stop (in children as in adults). They do not say what precise dosage to keep up for a lifetime: ask a professional if you are unsure.8,13
